text: What resources should people seek out if they want to learn more about a critical scholarly approach to the Bible? Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlelen. I'm a scholar
of the Bible and religion. And I get this question a lot. In fact, somebody asked this question last night at a book event here in Clarkdale, Arizona. And I
always start by recommending a good study Bible. And the one I recommend right now is the SPL Study Bible, which
has a lot of wonderful introductions to each book of the Bible that talk about authorship, that talk about date, that talk about literary style and rhetorical
goals and all that kind of stuff. It has wonderful explanatory notes in the bottom. It also has little mini essays in sidebars throughout the text. It also
incorporates the updated edition of the new revised standard version, the NRSVE, which is only a few years old.
Now, there's going to be a sixth edition of the new Oxford annotated Bible coming out within the next year or two that
will also incorporate the NRSVE into their own wonderful study Bible. So,
that will also be a very good study Bible when it comes out. And then there's also the Jewish study Bible that is in a second edition if you're looking
for just the Hebrew Bible. And I also recommend the Jewish annotated New Testament, which is the NRSV's New
Testament with commentary from Jewish scholars that uh set up the Jewish setting for what's being discussed in the New Testament and talk about how it
reflects certain Jewish perspectives from the first century CE. The next thing I usually recommend is a history
of the Bible, specifically the book, A History of the Bible by John Barton. The subtitle is the book and its faiths. I
think this is the best history of the Bible that is available today. It talks about where the Bible came from, talks about how it came together, how it was
canonized, and then how it has traditionally been read by both Jewish and Christian groups. Don't think you can do better than that for a history of the Bible. The next step, I would say,
would be good introductions to the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament. For the Hebrew Bible, John Collins's uh an

introduction to the Hebrew Bible has always been wonderful. It's in a third or fourth edition right now. I would highly recommend that one. And for the New Testament, I would recommend Bartman and Ugo Mendes's The New Testament,
which is in the eth edition, I believe.
And then the next step would be critical commentaries. And if you're just looking for the Torah, I would recommend the JPS Torah commentary series. I think that's
wonderful. And then they also have commentaries for the rest of the Tanakh.
